Note: All paths are relative. Some paths may contain wildcards (e.g., "folder/*" or "file-*.csv"). Use glob patterns to match and read those files.

Question: Using OMNI2 data, run the NRLMSISE-00 atmospheric model to predict neutral density values for Swarm-B throughout 2024. Derive model inputs (F10.7, F10.7A, daily Ap, 3-hour Ap vector) directly from the OMNI2 dataset. Compare predictions against measured neutral density from Swarm-B POD files and report RMSE over the entire year. Do not use external space weather feeds. OMNI2 data format specification can be found at omni2.text file. 3-hour AP defined according to https://www.mathworks.com/help/aeroblks/nrlmsise00atmospheremodel.html.

Answer format: The result should be a single number in scientific notation with 4 significant figures.

Your last line MUST BE: **Final Answer: <value>**

  The  /data/omni/low_res_omni/ directory contains the hourly mean values of 
  the interplanetary magnetic  field (IMF) and solar wind plasma parameters 
  measured by various spacecraft near  the  Earth's  orbit,  as  well  as  
  geomagnetic and solar activity indices, and energetic proton fluxes
  known as OMNI2 data. 

  OMNI2 was created at NSSDC in 2003 as a successor to the OMNI data set 
  first created in the mid-1970's.  
                   
  Time spans of various parameters are periodically extended.
   The documentation file at
    https://omniweb.gsfc.nasa.gov/html/ow_data.html
    gives the current time spans of the following parameter groups:
    Magnetic field
    Plasma
    Kp index and sunspot number
    AE, AL,AU index
    Provisional AE, AL, AU index
    Quick look AE, AL, AU index
    Dst index

    Quick look Dst
    Energetic proton fluxes
    ap-index and f10.7_index
    PC(N) index
 ---------------
 Note: see "extended" directoty for more parameters.
 ----------------------------------------------
 
  Data gaps were filled with dummy numbers for the missing hours or entire
  days to make all files of equal length.  The character '9' is used to
  fill all fields for missing data according to their format, e.g.
  ' 9999.9' for a field with the FORTRAN format F7.1. Note that format F7.1
  below really means (1X,F6.1),etc.

  This directory  includes  two types of the ASCII flat files: OMNI2_YYYY.DAT, 
  and OMNI_MYYYY.DAT  where  YYYY  is  a given year. The OMNI2_YYYY.DAT files 
  contain the original data where  the  IMF  and solar wind velocity vectors 
  are presented in GSE and, for IMF, GSM coordinate  systems.  The modified 
  OMNI_MYYYY.DAT files have been  created  from  these  files with reformatting 
  for COHOWeb compatibility and with the  IMF and velocity 
  vectors having been transformed to  RTN coordinate system. 
                            
--------------------------------------------------------------------------- 

Daily and 27-day Averages files: omni_01_av.dat; omni_27_av.dat; omni_m_daily.dat

We have computed daily and 27-day average values for all the OMNI parameters in the
OMNI2_YYYY.dat files, and we have computed daily averages from the OMNI_MYYYY.dat files.
We have made these lower resolution averages also accessible via OMNIWeb and via anon/ftp.
Only arithmetic averaging was done.  (No averaging of logarithms.)  No threshold numbers 
of finer scale points were required.


The daily averages are taken over OMNI's basic hourly values, and the 27-
day averages are taken over the daily averages.  The corresponding standard 
deviations relate only to these averagings and do not capture the 
variances in the higher resolution data.

The 27-day averages are for discrete Bartels rotation numbers.  Thus the 
first such average fully within 1999 spans January 9 through February 4.

The record format for the daily and 27-day averages is the same as for the 
hourly data, although certain fields have special meanings.

The time words (year, day, hour) correspond to the first hour of the 
average.

The ID's for the magnetic field and plasma spacecraft are set to zero, 
since the daily and 27-day averages frequently involve data from multiple 
spacecraft.

The numbers of fine scale points in the plasma and field averages are 
counts of (1) hourly values contributing to daily averages or (2) daily 
values contributing to 27-day averages.  NOTE THAT WE HAVE NOT REQUIRED ANY 
MINIMUM NUMBER OF POINTS TO COMPUTE AN AVERAGE.  For cases where there was 
only one point, the standard deviations were set to zero.

Kp was treated specially.  After determining daily or 27-averages from 
basic values such as 10 (1), 13 (1+), 17 (2-), 20 (2), the average was 
rounded to the nearest "standard value" of Kp (i.e., 10, 13, 17, 20, ...).  
For cases where the average was exactly in the middle between standard 
values (e.g., 15), the lower standard value (13 in this case) was used.

                  DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
 
  The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
  fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
  ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
  at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
  longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
  precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
  degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
  the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
  system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
  longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 

  The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
  is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
  the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
  product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
  spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
  are parallel.

  measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
  angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
  been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
  the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
  coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
  flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
  motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
  use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
  in the RTN system.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

def load() -> pd.DataFrame:
    path = Path('data/astronomy/input/omni2_low_res/omni2_2024.dat')
    # fixed-width per OMNI2 spec; use colspecs inferred from typical OMNI2 layout (55 words)
    # We'll parse by whitespace since fields are fixed but separated; robust to multiple spaces.
    df = pd.read_csv(path, delim_whitespace=True, header=None)
    # name columns 1..N
    df.columns = [f'w{i}' for i in range(1, df.shape[1]+1)]
    return df

Question: Using OMNI2 data, run the NRLMSISE-00 atmospheric model to predict neutral density values for Swarm-B throughout 2024. Derive model inputs (F10.7, F10.7A, daily Ap, 3-hour Ap vector) directly from the OMNI2 dataset. Compare predictions against measured neutral density from Swarm-B POD files and report RMSE over the entire year. Do not use external space weather feeds. OMNI2 data format specification can be found at omni2.text file. 3-hour AP defined according to https://www.mathworks.com/help/aeroblks/nrlmsise00atmospheremodel.html.

Answer format: The result should be a single number in scientific notation with 4 significant figures.

Your last line MUST BE: **Final Answer: <value>**

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.

    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e.

    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction

def process(swarmb_pod_files):
    import pandas as pd
    import numpy as np
    import glob
    import re

    paths = swarmb_pod_files['path'].tolist()
    dfs = []
    for p in paths:
        # Skip comment/header lines starting with # or %
        df = pd.read_csv(p, sep=r"\s+", comment='#', header=None, engine='python')
        # Heuristic: expect at least time + density + position. Keep all cols.
        df['source_path'] = p
        dfs.append(df)
    out = pd.concat(dfs, ignore_index=True)
    # Try to detect datetime column: if first 6 cols are Y M D h m s
    if out.shape[1] >= 7:
        # columns 0..5 likely date parts
        ymdhms = out.iloc[:,0:6]
        if np.issubdtype(ymdhms.dtypes[0], np.number):
            try:
                dt = pd.to_datetime(dict(year=out[0].astype(int), month=out[1].astype(int), day=out[2].astype(int),
                                         hour=out[3].astype(int), minute=out[4].astype(int), second=out[5].astype(int)), errors='coerce', utc=True)
                out.insert(0,'datetime',dt)
            except Exception:
                pass
    return out

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

def process(omni2024):
    import pandas as pd
    df = omni2024.copy()
    df.columns = [c.replace('w','') for c in df.columns]
    # rename key columns per spec (1-indexed)
    rename = {
        '1':'year','2':'doy','3':'hour',
        '39':'kp','50':'ap_daily','51':'f107','52':'pcn'
    }
    df = df.rename(columns=rename)
    # construct datetime
    dt = pd.to_datetime(df['year'].astype(int).astype(str), format='%Y') + pd.to_timedelta(df['doy'].astype(int)-1, unit='D') + pd.to_timedelta(df['hour'].astype(int), unit='h')
    df['datetime'] = dt
    # clean fill values
    for col, fill in [('ap_daily',999),('f107',999.9),('kp',99)]:
        if col in df.columns:
            df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce')
            df.loc[df[col]==fill, col] = pd.NA
    # hourly ap from kp (approx): OMNI provides only daily ap. We'll compute 3-hour ap from daily Ap using empirical split? 
    # But requirement: derive 3-hour Ap vector directly from OMNI2 dataset. OMNI2 hourly file lacks 3-hour ap; so use Kp to derive ap_3h via standard table.
    kp_map = {
        0:0,3:2,7:3,10:4,13:5,17:6,20:7,23:9,27:12,30:15,33:18,37:22,40:27,43:32,47:39,50:48,53:56,57:67,60:80,63:94,67:111,70:132,73:154,77:179,80:207,83:236,87:300,90:400
    }
    # kp in file like 33 for 3+; already integer
    df['ap_3h'] = df['kp'].map(kp_map)
    df.loc[df['kp'].isna(), 'ap_3h'] = pd.NA
    # compute F10.7A as 81-day centered running mean of daily F10.7 (use daily averages from hourly)
    daily = df.groupby(['year','doy'], as_index=False).agg({'f107':'mean','ap_daily':'mean'})
    daily['date'] = pd.to_datetime(daily['year'].astype(int).astype(str), format='%Y') + pd.to_timedelta(daily['doy'].astype(int)-1, unit='D')
    daily = daily.sort_values('date')
    daily['f107a'] = daily['f107'].rolling(window=81, center=True, min_periods=1).mean()
    daily = daily[['date','f107','f107a','ap_daily']]
    df = df.merge(daily, left_on=df['datetime'].dt.floor('D'), right_on='date', how='left', suffixes=('','_d'))
    df = df.drop(columns=['key_0','date'])
    return df[['datetime','f107_d','f107a','ap_daily_d','ap_3h']].rename(columns={'f107_d':'f107','ap_daily_d':'ap_daily'})
input.summary: Clean OMNI2 2024: parse datetime; extract F10.7 (w51), daily Ap (w50), Kp (w39); convert Kp->3h ap via standard table; compute F10.7A as 81-day centered running mean of daily F10.7 derived from hourly; output hourly table with datetime,f107,f107a,ap_daily,ap_3h

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

def process(omni2024):
    import pandas as pd
    df = omni2024.copy()
    df.columns = [c.replace('w','') for c in df.columns]
    rename = {'1':'year','2':'doy','3':'hour','39':'kp','50':'ap_daily','51':'f107'}
    df = df.rename(columns=rename)

    df['datetime'] = (
        pd.to_datetime(df['year'].astype(int).astype(str), format='%Y')
        + pd.to_timedelta(df['doy'].astype(int)-1, unit='D')
        + pd.to_timedelta(df['hour'].astype(int), unit='h')
    )

    # replace fill values with NA
    df['ap_daily'] = pd.to_numeric(df['ap_daily'], errors='coerce')
    df['f107'] = pd.to_numeric(df['f107'], errors='coerce')
    df['kp'] = pd.to_numeric(df['kp'], errors='coerce')
    df.loc[df['ap_daily']==999, 'ap_daily'] = pd.NA
    df.loc[df['f107']==999.9, 'f107'] = pd.NA
    df.loc[df['kp']==99, 'kp'] = pd.NA

    # Kp code to ap (3-hour) mapping (standard table)
    kp_map = {
        0:0, 3:2, 7:3, 10:4, 13:5, 17:6, 20:7, 23:9, 27:12, 30:15, 33:18, 37:22,
        40:27, 43:32, 47:39, 50:48, 53:56, 57:67, 60:80, 63:94, 67:111, 70:132,
        73:154, 77:179, 80:207, 83:236, 87:300, 90:400
    }
    df['ap_3h'] = df['kp'].map(kp_map).astype('float')

    # daily series for f107 and ap_daily
    daily = (df.groupby(['year','doy'], as_index=False)
               .agg(f107=('f107','mean'), ap_daily=('ap_daily','mean')))
    daily['date'] = (pd.to_datetime(daily['year'].astype(int).astype(str), format='%Y')
                     + pd.to_timedelta(daily['doy'].astype(int)-1, unit='D'))
    daily = daily.sort_values('date')
    daily['f107a'] = daily['f107'].rolling(window=81, center=True, min_periods=1).mean()

    df['date'] = df['datetime'].dt.floor('D')
    df = df.merge(daily[['date','f107a','f107','ap_daily']], on='date', how='left', suffixes=('','_d'))

    # after merge, keep daily-derived f107/ap as per model inputs
    out = df[['datetime','f107_d','f107a','ap_daily_d','ap_3h']].rename(
        columns={'f107_d':'f107','ap_daily_d':'ap_daily'}
    )
    return out
input.summary: Clean OMNI2 2024 hourly data: build datetime from year/doy/hour; replace fill values; compute 3-hour ap from Kp via standard table; compute daily f107 and 81-day centered f107a; output hourly datetime,f107,f107a,ap_daily,ap_3h

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

  Code: def process(omni2024):
    import pandas as pd
    df = omni2024.copy()
    df.columns = [c.replace('w','') for c in df.columns]
    # rename key columns per spec (1-indexed)
    rename = {
        '1':'year','2':'doy','3':'hour',
        '39':'kp','50':'ap_daily','51':'f107','52':'pcn'
    }
    df = df.rename(columns=rename)
    # construct datetime
    dt = pd.to_datetime(df['year'].astype(int).astype(str), format='%Y') + pd.to_timedelta(df['doy'].astype(int)-1, unit='D') + pd.to_timedelta(df['hour'].astype(int), unit='h')
    df['datetime'] = dt
    # clean fill values
    for col, fill in [('ap_daily',999),('f107',999.9),('kp',99)]:
        if col in df.columns:
            df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce')
            df.loc[df[col]==fill, col] = pd.NA
    # hourly ap from kp (approx): OMNI provides only daily ap. We'll compute 3-hour ap from daily Ap using empirical split? 
    # But requirement: derive 3-hour Ap vector directly from OMNI2 dataset. OMNI2 hourly file lacks 3-hour ap; so use Kp to derive ap_3h via standard table.
    kp_map = {
        0:0,3:2,7:3,10:4,13:5,17:6,20:7,23:9,27:12,30:15,33:18,37:22,40:27,43:32,47:39,50:48,53:56,57:67,60:80,63:94,67:111,70:132,73:154,77:179,80:207,83:236,87:300,90:400
    }
    # kp in file like 33 for 3+; already integer
    df['ap_3h'] = df['kp'].map(kp_map)
    df.loc[df['kp'].isna(), 'ap_3h'] = pd.NA
    # compute F10.7A as 81-day centered running mean of daily F10.7 (use daily averages from hourly)
    daily = df.groupby(['year','doy'], as_index=False).agg({'f107':'mean','ap_daily':'mean'})
    daily['date'] = pd.to_datetime(daily['year'].astype(int).astype(str), format='%Y') + pd.to_timedelta(daily['doy'].astype(int)-1, unit='D')
    daily = daily.sort_values('date')
    daily['f107a'] = daily['f107'].rolling(window=81, center=True, min_periods=1).mean()
    daily = daily[['date','f107','f107a','ap_daily']]
    df = df.merge(daily, left_on=df['datetime'].dt.floor('D'), right_on='date', how='left', suffixes=('','_d'))
    df = df.drop(columns=['key_0','date'])
    return df[['datetime','f107_d','f107a','ap_daily_d','ap_3h']].rename(columns={'f107_d':'f107','ap_daily_d':'ap_daily'})

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

def process(swarmb_dns):
    import pandas as pd
    df = swarmb_dns.copy()
    # First two columns in swarmb_dns are already date (datetime64 date) and time (datetime64 time)
    df = df.rename(columns={0:'date', 1:'time', 3:'alt_km', 4:'lon_deg', 5:'lat_deg', 6:'lst_hr', 8:'rho_meas'})

    # Build full UTC datetime
    date_str = pd.to_datetime(df['date'], errors='coerce').dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
    time_str = pd.to_datetime(df['time'], errors='coerce').dt.strftime('%H:%M:%S.%f')
    df['datetime'] = pd.to_datetime(date_str + ' ' + time_str, utc=True, errors='coerce')

    out = df[['datetime','alt_km','lat_deg','lon_deg','lst_hr','rho_meas']].copy()
    for c in ['alt_km','lat_deg','lon_deg','lst_hr','rho_meas']:
        out[c] = pd.to_numeric(out[c], errors='coerce')
    out = out.dropna(subset=['datetime','alt_km','lat_deg','lon_deg','rho_meas'])
    return out.sort_values('datetime').reset_index(drop=True)
input.summary: Parse Swarm-B POD DNS concatenated table: rename numeric columns, construct UTC datetime from separate date and time columns (already parsed as datetime types), and keep datetime/alt_km/lat_deg/lon_deg/llst_hr/rho_meas.

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

def process(swarmb_dns):
    import pandas as pd
    df = swarmb_dns.copy()
    # columns are labeled as integers and source_path
    df = df.rename(columns={0:'date', 1:'time', 3:'alt_km', 4:'lon_deg', 5:'lat_deg', 6:'lst_hr', 8:'rho_meas'})

    # Build full UTC datetime from date + time columns (both already datetime-like)
    date_part = pd.to_datetime(df['date'], errors='coerce').dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
    time_part = pd.to_datetime(df['time'], errors='coerce').dt.strftime('%H:%M:%S.%f')
    dt = pd.to_datetime(date_part + ' ' + time_part, utc=True, errors='coerce')

    out = pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': dt,
        'alt_km': pd.to_numeric(df['alt_km'], errors='coerce'),
        'lat_deg': pd.to_numeric(df['lat_deg'], errors='coerce'),
        'lon_deg': pd.to_numeric(df['lon_deg'], errors='coerce'),
        'lst_hr': pd.to_numeric(df['lst_hr'], errors='coerce'),
        'rho_meas': pd.to_numeric(df['rho_meas'], errors='coerce'),
    })
    out = out.dropna(subset=['datetime','alt_km','lat_deg','lon_deg','rho_meas'])
    return out.sort_values('datetime').reset_index(drop=True)

    are presented in GSE and, for IMF, GSM coordinate  systems.  The modified 
    OMNI_MYYYY.DAT files have been  created  from  these  files with reformatting 
    for COHOWeb compatibility and with the  IMF and velocity 
    vectors having been transformed to  RTN coordinate system. 
                              
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------- 
  
  Daily and 27-day Averages files: omni_01_av.dat; omni_27_av.dat; omni_m_daily.dat
  
  We have computed daily and 27-day average values for all the OMNI parameters in the
  OMNI2_YYYY.dat files, and we have computed daily averages from the OMNI_MYYYY.dat files.
  We have made these lower resolution averages also accessible via OMNIWeb and via anon/ftp.
  Only arithmetic averaging was done.  (No averaging of logarithms.)  No threshold numbers 
  of finer scale points were required.
  
  
  The daily averages are taken over OMNI's basic hourly values, and the 27-
  day averages are taken over the daily averages.  The corresponding standard 
  deviations relate only to these averagings and do not capture the 
  variances in the higher resolution data.
  
  The 27-day averages are for discrete Bartels rotation numbers.  Thus the 
  first such average fully within 1999 spans January 9 through February 4.
  
  The record format for the daily and 27-day averages is the same as for the 
  hourly data, although certain fields have special meanings.
  
  The time words (year, day, hour) correspond to the first hour of the 
  average.
  
  The ID's for the magnetic field and plasma spacecraft are set to zero, 
  since the daily and 27-day averages frequently involve data from multiple 
  spacecraft.
  
  The numbers of fine scale points in the plasma and field averages are 
  counts of (1) hourly values contributing to daily averages or (2) daily 
  values contributing to 27-day averages.  NOTE THAT WE HAVE NOT REQUIRED ANY 
  MINIMUM NUMBER OF POINTS TO COMPUTE AN AVERAGE.  For cases where there was 
  only one point, the standard deviations were set to zero.
  
  Kp was treated specially.  After determining daily or 27-averages from 
  basic values such as 10 (1), 13 (1+), 17 (2-), 20 (2), the average was 
  rounded to the nearest "standard value" of Kp (i.e., 10, 13, 17, 20, ...).  
  For cases where the average was exactly in the middle between standard 
  values (e.g., 15), the lower standard value (13 in this case) was used.

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

def process(swarmb_dns):
    import pandas as pd
    df = swarmb_dns.copy()

    # Identify actual column names (can be ints or strings like '0','1',...)
    cols = list(df.columns)
    def pick(name):
        return name if name in cols else (str(name) if str(name) in cols else None)

    c_date = pick(0)
    c_time = pick(1)
    c_alt  = pick(3)
    c_lon  = pick(4)
    c_lat  = pick(5)
    c_lst  = pick(6)
    c_rho  = pick(8)

    sub = df[[c_date, c_time, c_alt, c_lon, c_lat, c_lst, c_rho]].copy()
    sub.columns = ['date', 'time', 'alt_km', 'lon_deg', 'lat_deg', 'lst_hr', 'rho_meas']

    # Build UTC datetime
    # 'date' is date at 00:00:00; 'time' is time-of-day as datetime on an arbitrary date
    date_str = pd.to_datetime(sub['date'], errors='coerce').dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
    time_str = pd.to_datetime(sub['time'], errors='coerce').dt.strftime('%H:%M:%S.%f')
    dt = pd.to_datetime(date_str + ' ' + time_str, utc=True, errors='coerce')

    out = pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': dt,
        'alt_km': pd.to_numeric(sub['alt_km'], errors='coerce'),
        'lat_deg': pd.to_numeric(sub['lat_deg'], errors='coerce'),
        'lon_deg': pd.to_numeric(sub['lon_deg'], errors='coerce'),
        'lst_hr': pd.to_numeric(sub['lst_hr'], errors='coerce'),
        'rho_meas': pd.to_numeric(sub['rho_meas'], errors='coerce'),
    })
    out = out.dropna(subset=['datetime','alt_km','lat_deg','lon_deg','rho_meas'])
    out = out.sort_values('datetime').reset_index(drop=True)
    return out

    Data gaps were filled with dummy numbers for the missing hours or entire
    days to make all files of equal length.  The character '9' is used to
    fill all fields for missing data according to their format, e.g.
    ' 9999.9' for a field with the FORTRAN format F7.1. Note that format F7.1
    below really means (1X,F6.1),etc.
  
    This directory  includes  two types of the ASCII flat files: OMNI2_YYYY.DAT, 
    and OMNI_MYYYY.DAT  where  YYYY  is  a given year. The OMNI2_YYYY.DAT files 
    contain the original data where  the  IMF  and solar wind velocity vectors 
    are presented in GSE and, for IMF, GSM coordinate  systems.  The modified 
    OMNI_MYYYY.DAT files have been  created  from  these  files with reformatting 
    for COHOWeb compatibility and with the  IMF and velocity 
    vectors having been transformed to  RTN coordinate system. 
                              
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------- 
  
  Daily and 27-day Averages files: omni_01_av.dat; omni_27_av.dat; omni_m_daily.dat
  
  We have computed daily and 27-day average values for all the OMNI parameters in the
  OMNI2_YYYY.dat files, and we have computed daily averages from the OMNI_MYYYY.dat files.
  We have made these lower resolution averages also accessible via OMNIWeb and via anon/ftp.
  Only arithmetic averaging was done.  (No averaging of logarithms.)  No threshold numbers 
  of finer scale points were required.
  
  
  The daily averages are taken over OMNI's basic hourly values, and the 27-
  day averages are taken over the daily averages.  The corresponding standard 
  deviations relate only to these averagings and do not capture the 
  variances in the higher resolution data.
  
  The 27-day averages are for discrete Bartels rotation numbers.  Thus the 
  first such average fully within 1999 spans January 9 through February 4.
  
  The record format for the daily and 27-day averages is the same as for the 
  hourly data, although certain fields have special meanings.
  
  The time words (year, day, hour) correspond to the first hour of the 
  average.
  
  The ID's for the magnetic field and plasma spacecraft are set to zero, 
  since the daily and 27-day averages frequently involve data from multiple 
  spacecraft.
  
  The numbers of fine scale points in the plasma and field averages are 
  counts of (1) hourly values contributing to daily averages or (2) daily 
  values contributing to 27-day averages.  NOTE THAT WE HAVE NOT REQUIRED ANY 
  MINIMUM NUMBER OF POINTS TO COMPUTE AN AVERAGE.  For cases where there was 
  only one point, the standard deviations were set to zero.
  
  Kp was treated specially.  After determining daily or 27-averages from 
  basic values such as 10 (1), 13 (1+), 17 (2-), 20 (2), the average was 
  rounded to the nearest "standard value" of Kp (i.e., 10, 13, 17, 20, ...).  
  For cases where the average was exactly in the middle between standard 
  values (e.g., 15), the lower standard value (13 in this case) was used.

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

def process(swarmb_dns):
    import pandas as pd
    df = swarmb_dns

    # ensure column access
    cols = list(df.columns)
    def pick(k):
        return k if k in cols else (str(k) if str(k) in cols else None)

    c_date, c_time = pick(0), pick(1)
    c_alt, c_lon, c_lat, c_lst, c_rho = pick(3), pick(4), pick(5), pick(6), pick(8)

    sub = df[[c_date, c_time, c_alt, c_lon, c_lat, c_lst, c_rho]].copy()
    sub.columns = ['date', 'time', 'alt_km', 'lon_deg', 'lat_deg', 'lst_hr', 'rho_meas']

    # Build datetime efficiently
    d = pd.to_datetime(sub['date'], errors='coerce', utc=True)
    t = pd.to_datetime(sub['time'], errors='coerce')
    # time-of-day as timedelta
    td = pd.to_timedelta(t.dt.hour, unit='h') + pd.to_timedelta(t.dt.minute, unit='m') + pd.to_timedelta(t.dt.second, unit='s') + pd.to_timedelta(t.dt.microsecond, unit='us')
    dt = d + td

    out = pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': dt,
        'alt_km': pd.to_numeric(sub['alt_km'], errors='coerce'),
        'lat_deg': pd.to_numeric(sub['lat_deg'], errors='coerce'),
        'lon_deg': pd.to_numeric(sub['lon_deg'], errors='coerce'),
        'lst_hr': pd.to_numeric(sub['lst_hr'], errors='coerce'),
        'rho_meas': pd.to_numeric(sub['rho_meas'], errors='coerce'),
    })

    out = out.dropna(subset=['datetime','alt_km','lat_deg','lon_deg','rho_meas'])
    out = out.sort_values('datetime')

    # downsample to 1-minute to reduce size (Swarm is 30s cadence)
    out = out.set_index('datetime').resample('1min').mean(numeric_only=True).dropna(subset=['rho_meas']).reset_index()
    return out

    This directory  includes  two types of the ASCII flat files: OMNI2_YYYY.DAT, 
    and OMNI_MYYYY.DAT  where  YYYY  is  a given year. The OMNI2_YYYY.DAT files 
    contain the original data where  the  IMF  and solar wind velocity vectors 
    are presented in GSE and, for IMF, GSM coordinate  systems.  The modified 
    OMNI_MYYYY.DAT files have been  created  from  these  files with reformatting

  Daily and 27-day Averages files: omni_01_av.dat; omni_27_av.dat; omni_m_daily.dat
  
  We have computed daily and 27-day average values for all the OMNI parameters in the
  OMNI2_YYYY.dat files, and we have computed daily averages from the OMNI_MYYYY.dat files.
  We have made these lower resolution averages also accessible via OMNIWeb and via anon/ftp.
  Only arithmetic averaging was done.  (No averaging of logarithms.)  No threshold numbers 
  of finer scale points were required.
  
  
  The daily averages are taken over OMNI's basic hourly values, and the 27-
  day averages are taken over the daily averages.  The corresponding standard 
  deviations relate only to these averagings and do not capture the 
  variances in the higher resolution data.
  
  The 27-day averages are for discrete Bartels rotation numbers.  Thus the 
  first such average fully within 1999 spans January 9 through February 4.
  
  The record format for the daily and 27-day averages is the same as for the 
  hourly data, although certain fields have special meanings.
  
  The time words (year, day, hour) correspond to the first hour of the 
  average.
  
  The ID's for the magnetic field and plasma spacecraft are set to zero, 
  since the daily and 27-day averages frequently involve data from multiple 
  spacecraft.
  
  The numbers of fine scale points in the plasma and field averages are 
  counts of (1) hourly values contributing to daily averages or (2) daily 
  values contributing to 27-day averages.  NOTE THAT WE HAVE NOT REQUIRED ANY 
  MINIMUM NUMBER OF POINTS TO COMPUTE AN AVERAGE.  For cases where there was 
  only one point, the standard deviations were set to zero.
  
  Kp was treated specially.  After determining daily or 27-averages from 
  basic values such as 10 (1), 13 (1+), 17 (2-), 20 (2), the average was 
  rounded to the nearest "standard value" of Kp (i.e., 10, 13, 17, 20, ...).  
  For cases where the average was exactly in the middle between standard 
  values (e.g., 15), the lower standard value (13 in this case) was used.

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

    import pandas as pd
    df = swarmb_dns.copy()

    # Identify actual column names (can be ints or strings like '0','1',...)
    cols = list(df.columns)
    def pick(name):
        return name if name in cols else (str(name) if str(name) in cols else None)

    c_date = pick(0)
    c_time = pick(1)
    c_alt  = pick(3)
    c_lon  = pick(4)
    c_lat  = pick(5)
    c_lst  = pick(6)
    c_rho  = pick(8)

    sub = df[[c_date, c_time, c_alt, c_lon, c_lat, c_lst, c_rho]].copy()
    sub.columns = ['date', 'time', 'alt_km', 'lon_deg', 'lat_deg', 'lst_hr', 'rho_meas']

    # Build UTC datetime
    # 'date' is date at 00:00:00; 'time' is time-of-day as datetime on an arbitrary date
    date_str = pd.to_datetime(sub['date'], errors='coerce').dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
    time_str = pd.to_datetime(sub['time'], errors='coerce').dt.strftime('%H:%M:%S.%f')
    dt = pd.to_datetime(date_str + ' ' + time_str, utc=True, errors='coerce')

    out = pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': dt,
        'alt_km': pd.to_numeric(sub['alt_km'], errors='coerce'),
        'lat_deg': pd.to_numeric(sub['lat_deg'], errors='coerce'),

        'lst_hr': pd.to_numeric(sub['lst_hr'], errors='coerce'),

def process(swarmb_clean, omni_clean) -> pd.DataFrame:
    import pandas as pd
    df = swarmb_clean.copy()
    df['datetime_hour'] = df['datetime'].dt.floor('h')
    omni = omni_clean.copy()
    omni['datetime'] = pd.to_datetime(omni['datetime'], utc=True)
    out = df.merge(omni, left_on='datetime_hour', right_on='datetime', how='left', suffixes=('','_omni'))
    out = out.drop(columns=['datetime_omni'])
    return out

    fill all fields for missing data according to their format, e.g.
    ' 9999.9' for a field with the FORTRAN format F7.1. Note that format F7.1
    below really means (1X,F6.1),etc.
  
    This directory  includes  two types of the ASCII flat files: OMNI2_YYYY.DAT, 
    and OMNI_MYYYY.DAT  where  YYYY  is  a given year. The OMNI2_YYYY.DAT files 
    contain the original data where  the  IMF  and solar wind velocity vectors 
    are presented in GSE and, for IMF, GSM coordinate  systems.  The modified 
    OMNI_MYYYY.DAT files have been  created  from  these  files with reformatting 
    for COHOWeb compatibility and with the  IMF and velocity 
    vectors having been transformed to  RTN coordinate system. 
                              
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------- 
  
  Daily and 27-day Averages files: omni_01_av.dat; omni_27_av.dat; omni_m_daily.dat
  
  We have computed daily and 27-day average values for all the OMNI parameters in the
  OMNI2_YYYY.dat files, and we have computed daily averages from the OMNI_MYYYY.dat files.
  We have made these lower resolution averages also accessible via OMNIWeb and via anon/ftp.
  Only arithmetic averaging was done.  (No averaging of logarithms.)  No threshold numbers 
  of finer scale points were required.
  
  
  The daily averages are taken over OMNI's basic hourly values, and the 27-
  day averages are taken over the daily averages.  The corresponding standard 
  deviations relate only to these averagings and do not capture the 
  variances in the higher resolution data.
  
  The 27-day averages are for discrete Bartels rotation numbers.  Thus the 
  first such average fully within 1999 spans January 9 through February 4.
  
  The record format for the daily and 27-day averages is the same as for the 
  hourly data, although certain fields have special meanings.
  
  The time words (year, day, hour) correspond to the first hour of the 
  average.
  
  The ID's for the magnetic field and plasma spacecraft are set to zero, 
  since the daily and 27-day averages frequently involve data from multiple 
  spacecraft.
  
  The numbers of fine scale points in the plasma and field averages are 
  counts of (1) hourly values contributing to daily averages or (2) daily 
  values contributing to 27-day averages.  NOTE THAT WE HAVE NOT REQUIRED ANY 
  MINIMUM NUMBER OF POINTS TO COMPUTE AN AVERAGE.  For cases where there was 
  only one point, the standard deviations were set to zero.
  
  Kp was treated specially.  After determining daily or 27-averages from 
  basic values such as 10 (1), 13 (1+), 17 (2-), 20 (2), the average was 
  rounded to the nearest "standard value" of Kp (i.e., 10, 13, 17, 20, ...).  
  For cases where the average was exactly in the middle between standard 
  values (e.g., 15), the lower standard value (13 in this case) was used.

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

input.code:
def process(swarmb_clean, omni_clean) -> pd.DataFrame:
    import pandas as pd
    df = swarmb_clean.copy()
    # ensure timezone-aware UTC
    df['datetime'] = pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True)
    df['datetime_hour'] = df['datetime'].dt.floor('h')

    omni = omni_clean.copy()
    omni['datetime'] = pd.to_datetime(omni['datetime'], utc=True)

    out = df.merge(
        omni,
        left_on='datetime_hour',
        right_on='datetime',
        how='left',
        suffixes=('', '_omni')
    )
    out = out.drop(columns=['datetime_omni'])
    return out
input.summary: Join Swarm-B 1-min data to OMNI2 hourly inputs by flooring Swarm datetime to UTC hour; ensure both keys are tz-aware UTC; attach f107,f107a,ap_daily,ap_3h.

    and OMNI_MYYYY.DAT  where  YYYY  is  a given year. The OMNI2_YYYY.DAT files 
    contain the original data where  the  IMF  and solar wind velocity vectors

  Daily and 27-day Averages files: omni_01_av.dat; omni_27_av.dat; omni_m_daily.dat
  
  We have computed daily and 27-day average values for all the OMNI parameters in the
  OMNI2_YYYY.dat files, and we have computed daily averages from the OMNI_MYYYY.dat files.
  We have made these lower resolution averages also accessible via OMNIWeb and via anon/ftp.
  Only arithmetic averaging was done.  (No averaging of logarithms.)  No threshold numbers 
  of finer scale points were required.
  
  
  The daily averages are taken over OMNI's basic hourly values, and the 27-
  day averages are taken over the daily averages.  The corresponding standard 
  deviations relate only to these averagings and do not capture the 
  variances in the higher resolution data.
  
  The 27-day averages are for discrete Bartels rotation numbers.  Thus the 
  first such average fully within 1999 spans January 9 through February 4.
  
  The record format for the daily and 27-day averages is the same as for the 
  hourly data, although certain fields have special meanings.
  
  The time words (year, day, hour) correspond to the first hour of the 
  average.
  
  The ID's for the magnetic field and plasma spacecraft are set to zero, 
  since the daily and 27-day averages frequently involve data from multiple 
  spacecraft.
  
  The numbers of fine scale points in the plasma and field averages are 
  counts of (1) hourly values contributing to daily averages or (2) daily 
  values contributing to 27-day averages.  NOTE THAT WE HAVE NOT REQUIRED ANY 
  MINIMUM NUMBER OF POINTS TO COMPUTE AN AVERAGE.  For cases where there was 
  only one point, the standard deviations were set to zero.
  
  Kp was treated specially.  After determining daily or 27-averages from 
  basic values such as 10 (1), 13 (1+), 17 (2-), 20 (2), the average was 
  rounded to the nearest "standard value" of Kp (i.e., 10, 13, 17, 20, ...).  
  For cases where the average was exactly in the middle between standard 
  values (e.g., 15), the lower standard value (13 in this case) was used.

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

    f107a = df['f107a'].to_numpy(dtype=float)

    # ap vector definition (Matlab help): [dailyAp, ap(0-3), ap(3-6), ap(6-9), ap(9-12), ap(12-15), ap(15-18), ap(18-21)]

    ap3_series = omni_hourly.set_index('datetime_hour')['ap_3h']
    apd_series = omni_hourly.set_index('datetime_hour')['ap_daily']

    # For each sample time, we want 8-element ap vector at that hour:
    # [dailyAp, ap_current_bin, ap_prev1, ..., ap_prev6]
    # We'll compute by shifting ap3 at 3-hour resolution.

    ap3_3h = ap3_series.resample('3h').first()
    apd_1d = apd_series.resample('1d').first()

    for k in range(7):
        ap_vec[:, 1 + k] = ap3_3h.reindex(dt3 - pd.to_timedelta(3*k, unit='h')).to_numpy(dtype=float)

    # Fill any missing with current ap_3h and daily
    cur_ap3 = df['ap_3h'].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    cur_apd = df['ap_daily'].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    ap_vec[:, 0] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap_vec[:, 0]), ap_vec[:, 0], cur_apd)
    for j in range(1, 8):
        ap_vec[:, j] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap_vec[:, j]), ap_vec[:, j], cur_ap3)

    # Run MSIS. pymsis returns densities in kg/m^3? Actually pymsis returns number densities and mass density (g/cm^3?)
    # We'll request output and use total mass density 'rho' if provided.
    out = msis.run(t, lon, lat, alt_km, f107a=f107a, f107=f107, ap=ap_vec)

    # pymsis output is structured array with field 'rho' in kg/m^3
    try:
        rho_model = out['rho'].astype(float)
    except Exception:
        # fallback: last column
        rho_model = np.asarray(out)[..., -1].astype(float)

    res = pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True),
        'rho_meas': df['rho_meas'].to_numpy(dtype=float),
        'rho_model': rho_model,
    })

    # Some sw values might be in kg/m^3 already ~1e-12, so keep.
    return res

def process(join_inputs) -> pd.DataFrame:
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd

    from pymsis import msis

    df = join_inputs.copy()

    # times: datetime64[ns] naive UTC
    t = pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True).dt.tz_convert(None).to_numpy(dtype='datetime64[ns]')

    alt_km = df['alt_km'].to_numpy(float) / 1000.0  # meters -> km
    lat = df['lat_deg'].to_numpy(float)
    lon = df['lon_deg'].to_numpy(float)

    f107 = df['f107'].to_numpy(float)
    f107a = df['f107a'].to_numpy(float)

    # Construct 8-element ap vector per MATLAB definition
    dt_hour = pd.to_datetime(df['datetime_hour'], utc=True)
    omni_hourly = df[['datetime_hour', 'ap_3h', 'ap_daily']].drop_duplicates('datetime_hour').sort_values('datetime_hour')
    ap3_series = omni_hourly.set_index(pd.to_datetime(omni_hourly['datetime_hour'], utc=True))['ap_3h']
    apd_series = omni_hourly.set_index(pd.to_datetime(omni_hourly['datetime_hour'], utc=True))['ap_daily']

    ap3_3h = ap3_series.resample('3h').first()
    apd_1d = apd_series.resample('1D').first()

    dt3 = dt_hour.dt.floor('3h')
    dtd = dt_hour.dt.floor('1D')

    ap_vec = np.empty((len(df), 8), dtype=float)
    ap_vec[:, 0] = apd_1d.reindex(dtd).to_numpy(float)
    for k in range(7):
        ap_vec[:, 1 + k] = ap3_3h.reindex(dt3 - pd.to_timedelta(3*k, unit='h')).to_numpy(float)

    cur_ap3 = df['ap_3h'].to_numpy(float)
    cur_apd = df['ap_daily'].to_numpy(float)
    ap_vec[:, 0] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap_vec[:, 0]), ap_vec[:, 0], cur_apd)
    for j in range(1, 8):
        ap_vec[:, j] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap_vec[:, j]), ap_vec[:, j], cur_ap3)

    # pymsis API uses f107s (daily) and f107as (81-day avg)
    out = msis.run(t, lon, lat, alt_km, f107s=f107, f107as=f107a, aps=ap_vec)

    # out is xarray Dataset in newer versions; otherwise structured array
    rho_model = None
    if hasattr(out, 'keys') and ('rho' in out.keys()):
        rho_model = np.asarray(out['rho']).astype(float)
    else:
        try:
            rho_model = out['rho'].astype(float)
        except Exception:
            rho_model = np.asarray(out)[..., -1].astype(float)

    return pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True),
        'rho_meas': df['rho_meas'].to_numpy(float),
        'rho_model': rho_model,
    })

    f107 = df['f107'].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    f107a = df['f107a'].to_numpy(dtype=float)

    # ap vector definition (Matlab help): [dailyAp, ap(0-3), ap(3-6), ap(6-9), ap(9-12), ap(12-15), ap(15-18), ap(18-21)]
    # Here we only have current 3-hour ap. Construct a best-effort vector using historical 3h ap from previous 7 bins.
    # Build hourly index to map to omni hours, then compute 3-hour bins.
    dt_hour = pd.to_datetime(df['datetime_hour'], utc=True)
    # Create a mapping from hour to ap_3h and ap_daily
    omni_hourly = df[['datetime_hour', 'ap_3h', 'ap_daily']].drop_duplicates('datetime_hour').sort_values('datetime_hour')
    omni_hourly['bin'] = (omni_hourly['datetime_hour'].dt.hour // 3).astype(int)
    # Build per-hour ap_3h series
    ap3_series = omni_hourly.set_index('datetime_hour')['ap_3h']
    apd_series = omni_hourly.set_index('datetime_hour')['ap_daily']

    # For each sample time, we want 8-element ap vector at that hour:
    # [dailyAp, ap_current_bin, ap_prev1, ..., ap_prev6]
    # We'll compute by shifting ap3 at 3-hour resolution.
    # First resample to 3-hour grid at exact bin start times.
    ap3_3h = ap3_series.resample('3h').first()
    apd_1d = apd_series.resample('1d').first()

    # Align each sample time to its 3-hour bin start
    dt3 = dt_hour.dt.floor('3h')

    # Gather current and previous 6 bins
    ap_vec = np.empty((len(df), 8), dtype=float)
    # daily ap for that date
    dtd = dt_hour.dt.floor('1d')
    ap_vec[:, 0] = apd_1d.reindex(dtd).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    for k in range(7):
        ap_vec[:, 1 + k] = ap3_3h.reindex(dt3 - pd.to_timedelta(3*k, unit='h')).to_numpy(dtype=float)

    # Fill any missing with current ap_3h and daily
    cur_ap3 = df['ap_3h'].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    cur_apd = df['ap_daily'].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    ap_vec[:, 0] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap_vec[:, 0]), ap_vec[:, 0], cur_apd)

    # We'll request output and use total mass density 'rho' if provided.
    out = msis.run(t, lon, lat, alt_km, f107a=f107a, f107=f107, ap=ap_vec)

    # pymsis output is structured array with field 'rho' in kg/m^3
    try:

    except Exception:

        rho_model = np.asarray(out)[..., -1].astype(float)

        'datetime': pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True),
        'rho_meas': df['rho_meas'].to_numpy(dtype=float),
        'rho_model': rho_model,
    })

def process(join_inputs) -> pd.DataFrame:
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd
    from pymsis import msis

    df = join_inputs.copy()

    # times: datetime64[ns] naive UTC
    t = pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True).dt.tz_convert(None).to_numpy(dtype='datetime64[ns]')

    alt_km = df['alt_km'].to_numpy(float) / 1000.0  # meters -> km
    lat = df['lat_deg'].to_numpy(float)
    lon = df['lon_deg'].to_numpy(float)

    f107 = df['f107'].to_numpy(float)
    f107a = df['f107a'].to_numpy(float)

    # Build ap array per pymsis expected shape (n,7):
    # [dailyAp, current 3h, prev1..prev5] (total 7)
    dt_hour = pd.to_datetime(df['datetime_hour'], utc=True)

    omni_hourly = (
        df[['datetime_hour', 'ap_3h', 'ap_daily']]
        .drop_duplicates('datetime_hour')
        .sort_values('datetime_hour')
    )
    ap3_series = omni_hourly.set_index(pd.to_datetime(omni_hourly['datetime_hour'], utc=True))['ap_3h']
    apd_series = omni_hourly.set_index(pd.to_datetime(omni_hourly['datetime_hour'], utc=True))['ap_daily']

    ap3_3h = ap3_series.resample('3h').first()
    apd_1d = apd_series.resample('1D').first()

    dt3 = dt_hour.dt.floor('3h')
    dtd = dt_hour.dt.floor('1D')

    ap = np.empty((len(df), 7), dtype=float)
    ap[:, 0] = apd_1d.reindex(dtd).to_numpy(float)
    for k in range(6):
        ap[:, 1 + k] = ap3_3h.reindex(dt3 - pd.to_timedelta(3*k, unit='h')).to_numpy(float)

    cur_ap3 = df['ap_3h'].to_numpy(float)
    cur_apd = df['ap_daily'].to_numpy(float)
    ap[:, 0] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap[:, 0]), ap[:, 0], cur_apd)
    for j in range(1, 7):
        ap[:, j] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap[:, j]), ap[:, j], cur_ap3)

    out = msis.run(t, lon, lat, alt_km, f107s=f107, f107as=f107a, aps=ap)

    # Extract rho
    if hasattr(out, 'keys') and ('rho' in out.keys()):
        rho_model = np.asarray(out['rho']).astype(float)
    else:
        try:
            rho_model = out['rho'].astype(float)
        except Exception:
            rho_model = np.asarray(out).astype(float)

    rho_model = np.ravel(rho_model)

    return pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True),
        'rho_meas': df['rho_meas'].to_numpy(float),
        'rho_model': rho_model,
    })

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

def process(join_inputs) -> pd.DataFrame:
    import numpy as np
    import pandas as pd
    from pymsis import msis

    df = join_inputs.copy()

    # Build time/space arrays
    t = pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True).dt.tz_convert(None).to_numpy(dtype='datetime64[ns]')
    alt_km = df['alt_km'].to_numpy(float) / 1000.0  # meters -> km
    lat = df['lat_deg'].to_numpy(float)
    lon = df['lon_deg'].to_numpy(float)

    f107 = df['f107'].to_numpy(float)
    f107a = df['f107a'].to_numpy(float)

    # Prepare Ap time series from unique hours
    omni_hourly = (
        df[['datetime_hour', 'ap_3h', 'ap_daily']]
        .drop_duplicates('datetime_hour')
        .sort_values('datetime_hour')
    )
    omni_hourly['datetime_hour'] = pd.to_datetime(omni_hourly['datetime_hour'], utc=True)

    ap3_series = omni_hourly.set_index('datetime_hour')['ap_3h'].astype(float)
    apd_series = omni_hourly.set_index('datetime_hour')['ap_daily'].astype(float)

    # 3-hourly and daily series (aligned)
    ap3_3h = ap3_series.resample('3h').first()
    apd_1d = apd_series.resample('1D').first()

    dt_hour = pd.to_datetime(df['datetime_hour'], utc=True)
    dt3 = dt_hour.dt.floor('3h')
    dtd = dt_hour.dt.floor('1D')

    n = len(df)
    ap = np.empty((n, 7), dtype=float)
    ap[:, 0] = apd_1d.reindex(dtd).to_numpy()
    for k in range(6):
        ap[:, 1 + k] = ap3_3h.reindex(dt3 - pd.to_timedelta(3*k, unit='h')).to_numpy()

    # Fallbacks for any NaNs
    cur_ap3 = df['ap_3h'].to_numpy(float)
    cur_apd = df['ap_daily'].to_numpy(float)
    ap[:, 0] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap[:, 0]), ap[:, 0], cur_apd)
    for j in range(1, 7):
        ap[:, j] = np.where(np.isfinite(ap[:, j]), ap[:, j], cur_ap3)

    # Run MSIS
    out = msis.run(t, lon, lat, alt_km, f107s=f107, f107as=f107a, aps=ap)

    # Robust rho extraction
    rho_model = None
    if isinstance(out, dict):
        rho_model = out.get('rho', None)
    else:
        try:
            rho_model = out['rho']
        except Exception:
            rho_model = None

    if rho_model is None:
        rho_model = np.asarray(out)

    rho_model = np.asarray(rho_model).astype(float)
    # Reduce to (n,) if extra dims exist
    if rho_model.ndim == 2:
        if rho_model.shape[0] == n and rho_model.shape[1] == 1:
            rho_model = rho_model[:, 0]
        elif rho_model.shape[1] == n and rho_model.shape[0] == 1:
            rho_model = rho_model[0, :]
        else:
            # take first column as best guess
            rho_model = rho_model[:, 0]
    elif rho_model.ndim > 2:
        rho_model = rho_model.reshape((n, -1))[:, 0]

    # Ensure length n
    if len(rho_model) != n:
        raise ValueError(f"rho_model length {len(rho_model)} != n {n}; rho_model shape={rho_model.shape}")

    return pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True).to_numpy(),
        'rho_meas': df['rho_meas'].to_numpy(float),
        'rho_model': rho_model,
    })

                    DESCRIPTION OF COORDINATE SYSTEMS
   
    The Heliographic Inertial (HGI) coordinates are Sun-centered and inertially
    fixed with respect to an X-axis directed along the intersection line of the
    ecliptic and solar equatorial  planes. The solar equator plane is inclined
    at 7.25 degrees from the ecliptic. This direction was towards ecliptic 
    longitude of 74.367 degrees  on  1  January  1900  at  1200  UT; because of
    precession of the celestial  equator, this longitude increases by 1.4 
    degrees/century. The Z axis  is  directed perpendicular and northward from 
    the solar equator, and the  Y-axis  completes  the right-handed set. This 
    system differs from the usual  heliographic  coordinates  (e.g.  Carrington
    longitudes) which are fixed in the frame of the rotating Sun. 
  
    The RTN system is fixed at a spacecraft (or the planet). The R  axis 
    is directed radially away from the Sun, the T axis is the cross product of 
    the solar rotation axis and  the  R  axis,  and  the  N  axis is the cross 
    product of the R  and  T  axes.  At  zero  heliographic latitude, when the 
    spacecraft is in the solar equatorial plane, the N and solar rotation axes 
    are parallel.
                        
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                   Convention for Latitude and Longitude Angles
    --------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                         
    Latitude  and  longitude  angles  of  solar wind plasma flow are generally
    measured  from the radius vector away from the Sun. In all cases, latitude
    angles  are  positive for north-going flow. The flow longitude angles have
    been  treated differently for the near-Earth data, i.e. the OMNI, and for 
    the deep space data. The flow is positive for  the  near-Earth  data  when
    coming from the right side of the Sun as viewed  from  the Earth, i.e. 
    flowing toward +Y from -X GSE or opposite to the  direction of planetary 
    motion. On the other hand, the flow longitudes for the deep space spacecraft
    use the opposite sign convection, i.e. positive for flow in the +T direction
    in the RTN system.

    ap3_3h = ap3_series.resample('3h').first()
    apd_1d = apd_series.resample('1D').first()

    dt3 = dt_hour.dt.floor('3h')

    ap = np.empty((len(df), 7), dtype=float)
    ap[:, 0] = apd_1d.reindex(dtd).to_numpy(float)
    for k in range(6):

    cur_apd = df['ap_daily'].to_numpy(float)

    rho_model = np.ravel(rho_model)

    return pd.DataFrame({
        'datetime': pd.to_datetime(df['datetime'], utc=True),

  We have computed daily and 27-day average values for all the OMNI parameters in the
  OMNI2_YYYY.dat files, and we have computed daily averages from the OMNI_MYYYY.dat files.
  We have made these lower resolution averages also accessible via OMNIWeb and via anon/ftp.
  Only arithmetic averaging was done.  (No averaging of logarithms.)  No threshold numbers 
  of finer scale points were required.
  
  
  The daily averages are taken over OMNI's basic hourly values, and the 27-
  day averages are taken over the daily averages.  The corresponding standard 
  deviations relate only to these averagings and do not capture the 
  variances in the higher resolution data.
  
  The 27-day averages are for discrete Bartels rotation numbers.  Thus the 
  first such average fully within 1999 spans January 9 through February 4.
  
  The record format for the daily and 27-day averages is the same as for the 
  hourly data, although certain fields have special meanings.
  
  The time words (year, day, hour) correspond to the first hour of the 
  average.

  since the daily and 27-day averages frequently involve data from multiple 
  spacecraft.
